*Sì Shí* (The Four Seasons)
Spring water fills the four marshes,
summer clouds have many strange peaks.
The autumn moon raises its bright splendor,
and the winter peaks display solitary pines.
Number One
*Nǐ Gǔ Jiǔ Shǒu* (Nine Poems in the Ancient Style)
Luxuriant orchids grow under the window,
and dense willows stand before the hall.
When I first parted from you,
I did not think the journey would be so long.
Setting out as a traveler of ten thousand *lǐ*,
I met a good friend along the way.
We had not yet spoken and become drunk at heart,
and we were not joining in drinking cups of wine.
The orchids have withered and the willows have also declined,
and this has caused these words to be in vain.
Many thanks to the young men,
for knowing each other is not faithful and generous.
Their spirit and ambition overturn people's lives,
what more can separation bring?
Number Two
Leaving home early, I seriously prepared my carriage,
resolved to travel with a purpose, never to give up.
May I ask, sir, where are you going now?
It's neither for commerce nor for war.
I've heard of Tián Zǐtài,
whose integrity and righteousness made him a hero among scholars.
Though this man has long been dead,
the villagers still follow his example.
In life, he had a reputation that surpassed the world,
and after death, his fame is endlessly passed on.
I do not emulate those wild and reckless fellows,
but live honestly within the span of a hundred years.
Number Three
In the second month of spring, we meet with timely rains,
and the first thunder rumbles from the eastern corner.
All hibernating creatures are startled from their hiding places,
and grasses and trees stretch out freely.
Graceful, the new swallows arrive,
in pairs, entering my humble dwelling.
Their old nest is still there,
and they return together to their former home.
Since we parted ways,
the courtyard has become desolate day by day.
My heart is certainly not made of stone,
but what is your feeling like?
Number Four
High, high above, a hundred-foot tower,
clearly looking out over the four wildernesses.
At dusk, it becomes the home of returning clouds,
and at dawn, a hall for flying birds.
Mountains and rivers fill my eyes,
only the plains are a boundless expanse.
Scholars of ancient times, seeking fame and glory,
contended ardently for this arena;
but once a hundred years have passed,
they all return together to Běimáng.
Pine and cypress trees are felled by men,
and high tombs rise and fall against each other;
the ruined foundations have no remaining owner,
and where are the wandering souls?
Wealth and glory are indeed valuable,
but also pitiable and sad!
Number Five
In the east, there is a scholar,
whose clothing is often incomplete.
He eats only nine times every thirty days,
and wears the same hat for ten years.
No one suffers like this,
yet he always has a pleasant countenance.
I want to see this man,
and go beyond the Hé River pass at dawn.
Green pines grow along the road,
and white clouds lodge at the edge of his eaves.
Knowing my purpose in coming,
he takes out his zither to play for me:
the upper string startles a departing crane,
and the lower string plays a melody of a lonely phoenix.
I wish to stay and live with you,
from now until the cold of winter.
Number Six
The trees in the green valley,
are always the same, winter and summer.
They see frost and snow every year,
who says they do not know the season?
Tired of hearing the words of the world,
I made friends in Línzī;
many debaters are in Jìxià,
they will point out and resolve my doubts.
The preparations have been made for days,
and I have already said goodbye to my family;
walking, walking, I stopped at the door,
then sat back down, thinking again.
Not complaining about the length of the road,
but fearing that others will deceive me;
if it doesn't go as planned,
I will be laughed at by the world forever.
These feelings are difficult to express fully,
so I write this poem for you.
Number Seven
At dusk, the sky is without clouds,
and the spring breeze gently stirs.
A beautiful woman enjoys the clear night,
carousing and singing until dawn.
After the song, she sighs deeply,
holding this feeling moves many people.
The bright moon in the clouds,
and the bright flowers among the leaves,
how can there not be a moment of beauty,
but what will happen after a short time?
Number Eight
In my youth, I was strong and vigorous,
stroking my sword, I traveled alone.
Who says my travels were nearby?
From Zhāngyè to Yōuzhōu.
When hungry, I ate the ferns of Shǒuyáng,
and when thirsty, I drank from the Yì River.
I see no one who understands me,
I only see the ancient hills.
Two tall graves by the roadside,
belong to Bóyá and Zhuāng Zhōu.
Such scholars are hard to find again,
what am I seeking in my travels?
Number Nine
Planting mulberry trees by the Cháng River,
I hoped to harvest them in three years.
The branches and leaves were just beginning to flourish,
when suddenly the mountains and rivers changed.
The branches and leaves are broken and scattered,
and the roots float in the vast sea.
The spring silkworms have nothing to eat,
who will I wait for to make winter clothes?
Originally, I did not plant them on high ground,
what regrets do I have today!
Number One
*Miscellaneous Poems, Twelve Pieces*
Human life has no roots or stems,
drifting like dust on the road.
Scattered and driven by the wind,
this is no longer my own body.
Once we fall to earth, we are all brothers,
why must we be related by blood!
When there is joy, we should make merry,
gathering our neighbors for a jug of wine.
Our prime years will not come again,
and a single day will not dawn twice;
we should strive to make the most of our time,
for the years do not wait for us.
Number Two
The white sun sinks in the western river,
and the pale moon rises over the eastern hills.
Shining remotely for ten thousand miles,
a vast scene in the empty sky.
The wind comes in through the doors and windows,
and the pillow and mat are cold in the night.
I realize that the seasons are changing,
and staying awake, I know the night is long.
I want to speak but have no one to join me,
so I wave my cup, urging my lonely shadow.
The sun and moon fling us away,
and those with ambition cannot give full play.
Thinking of this, I feel sad and grieved,
and cannot find peace until dawn.
Number Three
Wealth and glory are hard to maintain for long,
and rise and fall cannot be measured.
In the past, I was a lotus of the third spring,
now I have become an autumn lotus seedpod.
Harsh frost freezes the wild grass,
but its withered state does not end quickly.
The sun and moon have their cycles,
but when I go, I will not return to the sunlight,
thinking fondly of the past,
remembering this breaks my heart.
Number Four
A man's ambition is to roam the four seas,
I wish not to know old age.
Relatives live together in one place,
and children and grandchildren protect each other.
We enjoy ourselves with wine and music, from sunrise to sunset,
and the wine in the jar never runs dry.
Relaxing our belts, we enjoy ourselves to the fullest,
rising late and sleeping early.
Who is like the men of today,
with hearts full of ice and burning coal?
After a hundred years, we return to the grave,
what is the use of empty fame!
Number Five
Remembering my youth,
I was happy and cheerful without any reason.
My fierce ambition soared over the four seas,
and my soaring wings longed to fly far away.
As the years passed by, I declined,
and that ambition has gradually faded;
when I encounter joy, I no longer feel entertained,
and am often filled with worries.
My strength is gradually weakening,
and I feel that each day is worse than the last.
A boat in a ravine cannot stop even for a moment,
pulling me along without letting me stay.
How much further is the road ahead?
I do not know where my final mooring place will be.
The ancients cherished every inch of time,
thinking of this makes me afraid.
Number Six
In the past, I heard elders say things that
I was always displeased to cover my ears against.
How could it be that after fifty years,
I suddenly find myself involved in these very things?
Seeking the joys of my prime,
I no longer have any inclination toward them.
Going, going, I want to go further away,
How could this life be worth living again?
Squandering my family's wealth for fleeting pleasures,
I let the years slip by so swiftly.
Not leaving gold for my sons,
What use would it be to leave it behind after my death!
Number Seven
The sun and moon do not linger,
The four seasons press each other urgently.
Cold winds brush against withered branches,
Fallen leaves cover the long streets.
My weak body declines with the times,
My dark temples have long since turned white.
A white marker is planted in people's hair,
The road ahead gradually narrows.
Home is like an inn for travelers,
I am like a guest who is about to depart.
Going, going, where do I want to go?
At Nán Shān 南山, there is an old home.
Number Eight
To till the fields as a substitute was never my expectation,
My work lies in the fields of mulberry and hemp.
I have never been remiss in personally taking care of it,
But I am still often cold and hungry, eating only dregs and husks.
I never expected to have a full belly,
I only wish to be full of rice.
Enough coarse cloth to withstand the winter,
Coarse linen to meet the spring.
Even this I cannot obtain,
Alas, how sad it is!
Everyone else obtains what is proper,
My clumsy life has lost its way.
What can reason do about it?
Let me make a cup of wine.
Number Nine
Far away, I follow the life of a sojourner,
My heart is in two places at once.
Wiping away tears, I sail eastward,
Following the current, I chase after the passage of time.
The sun has set, and the stars are 昴 (Mǎo),
Their light obscured by the peaks of Xī Shān 西山.
Desolate, I am separated by the edge of the sky,
Melancholy thoughts are my constant fare.
Filled with emotion, I think of returning south,
But the road is long, and I have no way to go.
Barriers and bridges are hard to circumvent,
So I send this poem as my only voice.
Number Ten
Living in leisure, I maintain my roaming spirit,
But time flies and cannot be stopped.
Driven by duties without rest,
The carriage hurries to the eastern cliffs.
Deep shade is like fragrant musk,
Cold air excites my heart.
The years have their constant order,
My stay here has been long and drawn out.
Stirred, I remember our close ties,
But this affection has long since departed.
Insensibly, ten years have passed,
I am temporarily bound by others.
The courtyard is shaded by remaining trees,
Suddenly, the sun and moon wane.
Number Eleven
My journey has not been far,
But looking back, the wind feels bleak and cold.
Spring swallows rise in season,
Flying high, they brush the dusty beams.
Border geese sadly have nowhere to go,
Changing seasons, they return to their northern lands;
Abandoned *kun* birds cry in clear ponds,
Passing through summer heat and autumn frost.
A sorrowful man finds words difficult,
The long spring night stretches endlessly.
Number Twelve
Graceful pine branches and sparrows,
Gentle and lovely young children.
They are only three to five years old,
How can they rely on tall trees?
Nourishing their color, they contain vital energy,
Brightly, they possess a sense of order.
Number One
*Yǒng Pín Shì Qī Shǒu* 詠貧士七首 (Seven Poems on Poor Scholars)
All beings have something to rely on,
Only solitary clouds have no support.
Dimly, they vanish in the air,
When will we see their remaining light?
Morning clouds dispel the overnight mist,
Many birds fly together;
Slowly their wings emerge from the forest,
Before dusk, they return again.
Measuring my strength, I keep to my old path,
How could I not be cold and hungry?
If sympathetic souls do not exist,
That's the end of it, what is there to grieve?
Number Two
The year ends, bleak and severe,
Embracing my coat, I bask in the sun before the eaves.
In the southern garden, there are no remaining blossoms,
Withered branches fill the northern garden.
I pour the pot, and there are no remaining drops,
I peek into the stove and see no smoke.
Poetry and books block the space outside my seat,
Even at sunset, I have no time to study them.
Living in leisure is not facing adversity,
But I secretly harbor grievances.
How can I comfort my heart?
I rely on the fact that many worthy men of old were like this.
Number Three
Róng Sǒu 榮叟, old and wearing a rope as a belt,
Happily plays the zither;
Yuán Shēng 原生 mends his worn-out shoes,
And sings a clear song in the *shāng* 商 tone.
Shùn 舜 is long gone,
And poor scholars search for each other through the generations.
The worn sleeve cannot cover the elbow,
And the *lí* 藜 broth is often too little to ladle out.
How could I forget putting on light furs?
What I would get would not be what I admire.
Cì 賜 could only argue skillfully,
But he could not see my heart.
Number Four
Content in poverty and guarding lowliness,
From ancient times, there was Qián Lóu 黔婁.
I do not glory in a good rank,
I do not repay a generous gift.
Once my life comes to an end,
My worn-out clothes will still be incomplete.
How could I not know its extremity,
But if it's not the right path, I have no worries.
Since the time of thousands of years ago,
I have not seen his like again.
Living in the morning with benevolence and righteousness,
Dying in the evening, what more could I ask for?
Number Five
Yuán Ān 袁安, trapped in deep snow,
Is distant and cannot be bothered;
When Ruan Gong 阮公 sees money coming in,
He abandons his official post that very day.
Straw has a constant warmth,
Gathering *jǔ* 莒 is enough for morning sustenance.
How could it not be truly bitter?
What I fear is not hunger and cold.
Poverty and wealth are constantly at war,
But when the Way prevails, there is no sadness.
His supreme virtue crowns the neighborhood,
And his pure integrity reflects on the western gate.
Number Six
Zhòng Yù 仲蔚 loves to live in poverty,
Around his house, artemisia and wormwood grow.
Hidden away, he cuts off social contacts,
And composes poems with considerable skill.
The whole world does not know him,
Except for one Liú Gǒng 劉龔.
Why is this gentleman so unique?
It is truly because he is rarely like others.
He rests content in his work,
And his joy is not in poverty or success.
Dealing with people is certainly clumsy,
But at least I can be with him for a long time.
Number Seven
In the past, there was Huáng Zǐlián 黃子廉,
Who brushed off his hat and assisted a famous governor.
One day he resigned his post and returned home,
His pure poverty was scarcely matched.
In a year of famine, his kind wife was moved,
And tears flowed toward me.
Although a man has ambition,
He is certainly concerned for his children.
Huì Sūn 惠孫 sighed once we met,
And his generous gifts were never repaid.
Who says that enduring poverty is difficult?
Distant indeed are those former worthies.
*Yǒng Èr Shū* 詠二疏 (Ode to the Two Shū)
The great phenomenon revolves through the four seasons,
those who accomplish merit depart of their own accord.
May I ask, since the decline of the Zhōu dynasty,
how many people have understood this principle?
Looking around the Hàn court,
the Èr Shū once again performed this act.
They returned to their old homes with a loud whistle,
and respectfully bowed to the tutor of the crown prince.
The entire imperial court saw them off,
and ornate carriages filled the roads.
The sorrow of parting was deeply felt,
but the remaining glory was not worth considering.
Their actions moved the travelers,
and their virtue was not just ordinary praise!
They happily enjoyed the pleasures of their villages,
and what they were doing was not focused on immediate affairs.
They urged the old men to draw closer,
and raised their cups, speaking of common matters.
Asking about gold, they finally entrusted their hearts,
and their pure words revealed what had not been understood.
They freely enjoyed their remaining years,
not worrying about what would happen after their deaths.
Who says those men have passed away?
Over time, their Dao becomes even more evident.
*Yǒng Sān Liáng* (Ode to the Three Good Men)
They dusted off their hats and rode to the ford,
only fearing that the times would leave them behind.
They diligently served through the years,
always worried that their merit was becoming insignificant.
Their loyalty was mistakenly revealed,
and they became favored by their lord.
When he went out, they accompanied his ornamented carriage,
and when he entered, they attended him behind the red curtains;
their advice was always followed,
and their plans were never flawed.
Once he passed away,
they wished to return with him.
His great kindness was certainly hard to forget,
but how could they disobey the lord's command!
Standing at the edge of the grave, they had no doubts,
and cast themselves into righteousness with hopeful hearts.
Thorns surround the tall tomb,
and the yellow birds sing with sorrow.
These good men cannot be redeemed,
and tears soak my clothes.
*Yǒng Jīng Kē* (Ode to Jīng Kē)
Yān Dān was good at fostering talent,
and his ambition was to repay the powerful Yíng.
He gathered the best men,
and at the end of the year, he obtained Jīng Qīng.
A gentleman dies for his confidant,
so he drew his sword and left Yān's capital;
a white horse neighed on the broad road,
and with fervor, saw me off.
His spirited hair pointed to his high hat,
and fierce energy filled his long tassel.
We drank farewell wine on the Yì River,
and heroes were arrayed in the four seats.
Jiàn Lí struck the mournful *zhù*,
and Sòng Yì sang in a loud voice.
The whistling, sorrowful wind passed,
and faint, cold waves arose.
The *shāng* note caused more tears to flow,
and the *yǔ* note startled the brave warriors.
His heart knew he would not return,
but he would have a name for later generations.
When would he look back at his carriage?
His flying cover entered the Qín court.
He fiercely crossed ten thousand *lǐ*,
and leisurely passed a thousand cities.
When the map was unrolled, the matter itself arrived,
and the powerful lord was startled and anxious.
Alas, his swordsmanship was unskilled,
and his extraordinary deed was not accomplished!
Although that man has already perished,
for a thousand years, there is still lingering emotion.
Number One
*Dú Shānhǎijīng Shísān Shǒu* (Thirteen Poems on Reading the Classic of Mountains and Seas)
In early summer, the grasses and trees grow,
and the trees around the house spread out.
The birds are happy to have a place to rest,
and I also love my dwelling.
I have already plowed and planted,
and sometimes I return to read my books.
The deep lane is separated by ruts,
but often, old friends' carriages turn back.
Happily, I pour spring wine,
and pick vegetables from my garden.
Light rain comes from the east,
and a good wind accompanies it.
I broadly read the *Biography of King Zhōu*,
and leisurely look at the *Maps of Mountains and Seas*.
Looking up and down, I encompass the universe,
what could be more joyful?
Number Two
The Jade Terrace towers, radiant and beautiful,
and the Wángmǔ has a joyful, wondrous face.
They were born together with Heaven and Earth,
and I don't know how many years have passed.
Her spiritual transformations are endless,
and her palaces are not on just one mountain.
Drunk and happy, I utter new songs,
not imitating the words of the common people.
Number Three
Distant and towering is the Huái River Ridge,

*Record of the Peach Blossom Spring, with a Poem*
During the Tài Yuán period of the Jìn Dynasty,
a man of Wǔlíng made fishing his occupation.
He traveled along the stream,
forgetting how far he had gone.
Suddenly, he encountered a peach blossom forest on both banks,
for several hundred paces, there were no other trees,
fragrant grass, fresh and beautiful,
fallen petals fluttering.
The fisherman found it very strange.
He continued forward,
wanting to reach the end of the forest.
At the end of the forest was the source of the stream,
and he found a mountain.
The mountain had a small opening,
seeming as if there was light.
He abandoned his boat and entered the opening.
At first, it was extremely narrow,
barely allowing a person through.
After walking several dozen paces,
it suddenly opened up and became bright.
The land was flat and wide,
houses and dwellings neatly arranged.
There were fine fields, beautiful ponds, mulberry and bamboo groves.
Paths between fields connected,
the sounds of chickens and dogs could be heard.
Among them, people came and went, planting and working,
the clothes of the men and women were all like those of outsiders.
The elderly with yellowed hair and children with their hair in tufts,
all content and joyful.
Seeing the fisherman,
they were greatly surprised.
They asked where he came from,
and he answered in detail.
They invited him to their home,
set out wine, killed chickens, and made a meal.
When the villagers heard of this person,
they all came to inquire.
They said that their ancestors, during the chaos of the Qín Dynasty,
led their wives, children, and fellow villagers,
to this isolated place,
and never left again,
thus becoming separated from outsiders.
When asked what dynasty it was now,
they did not even know of the Hàn Dynasty,
let alone the Wèi and Jìn Dynasties.
The fisherman told them everything he had heard,
and they all sighed in dismay.
Other people invited him to their homes,
and all brought out wine and food.
After staying for several days,
he took his leave.
The people in this place said,
"It is not worth telling outsiders."
After he left,
he found his boat,
and followed the path he had taken,
marking the places everywhere.
When he reached the prefecture,
he went to see the governor and told him everything.
The governor immediately sent someone to follow him,
to find the places he had marked,
but they became lost and could not find the way again.
Liú Zǐjì of Nányáng
was a noble and virtuous man.
Hearing of this,
he happily went there himself,
but did not succeed,
and soon died of illness.
Afterwards, there were no more who sought the ford.
Yíng's clan disrupted the order of the heavens,
and the virtuous fled their times.
The gentlemen of Huáng Qǐ, the Shāng Mountains,
those people also departed.
Past traces gradually faded,
and the paths that led here became overgrown and abandoned.
They encouraged each other to diligently farm,
and rested when the sun set.
Mulberry and bamboo cast lingering shade,
beans and millet were planted in season.
Spring silkworms produced long silk,
and in autumn, there were no taxes for the king.
The rough paths were dimly connected,
and the chickens and dogs barked at each other.
The sacrificial vessels and regulations were still those of ancient times,
and the clothing had no new designs.
Children freely sang as they walked,
and the gray-haired joyfully went out for excursions.
The flourishing of the grass revealed the harmony of the seasons,
and the withering of the trees revealed the force of the wind.
Although there were no records of years and months,
the four seasons formed a year by themselves.
Content and with abundant joy,
why bother with wisdom?
Strange traces were hidden for five hundred years,
and one morning, the realm of the gods was revealed.
Purity and vulgarity were from different origins,
and soon it returned to its secluded hiding.
May I ask, wandering scholar,
how can you fathom what is beyond the dust and noise?
I wish to step on the light wind,
and soar high to seek my companion.

*Guī Qù Lái Xī Cí*
My family was poor,
and farming was not enough to support myself.
Young children filled the room,
and the jars had no stored grain.
The means for making a living
I had not yet found the way.
Many relatives and friends advised me to become a magistrate.
I felt a sudden impulse
but could find no path to it.
Then there happened to be a recruitment from various places.
The regional governors regarded kindness and love as virtue.
My paternal uncle considered my poverty and hardship
and consequently I was employed in a small town.
At that time, the disturbances were not yet quelled.
My heart feared distant service.
Péngzé was a hundred *lǐ* from my home.
The profit from the public fields
was enough to make wine.
Therefore, I conveniently sought the position.
After a few days,
I felt a longing for the feeling of returning home.
Why?
My essential nature is natural,
not something obtained through forced effort.
Although hunger and cold are pressing,
going against myself brings multiple illnesses.
Having once engaged in worldly affairs,
I was entirely enslaved by my mouth and stomach.
Thereupon, I was filled with disappointment and indignation,
deeply ashamed of the ambitions of my life.
I still hoped for one harvest
and would then gather my clothes and leave by night.
Soon, my cousin Chéng's sister died in Wǔchāng.
My heart was set on rushing to her aid,
and I resigned from my post.
From mid-autumn to winter,
I was in office for more than eighty days.
Taking advantage of events to follow my heart,
I composed a poem entitled *Guī Qù Lái Xī*.
It was the eleventh month of the year *yǐsì*.
Return, oh, return!
My fields and garden are about to become overgrown; why not return?
Since I have already allowed my mind to be enslaved by my body,
why be sad and grieve alone?
I realize that the past cannot be corrected,
and know that the future can be pursued.
Indeed, I have not strayed far from the path.
I realize that today is right and yesterday was wrong.
The boat sways lightly as it sails,
and the wind gently blows my clothes.
I ask the traveler about the road ahead,
regretting the faint light of dawn.
Then I see my humble house,
filled with joy, I run.
The servants welcome me,
and the young children wait at the door.
The three paths are becoming overgrown,
but the pines and chrysanthemums still remain.
I lead the children into the room,
where wine fills the jug.
I take up the cup and pour myself a drink,
glancing at the branches of the trees in the courtyard with a happy face.
I lean on the south window to express my pride,
knowing that a small space is easily comfortable.
Daily strolls in the garden become a pleasure,
and though a door is provided, it is always closed.
I lean on my cane and wander about, resting,
occasionally raising my head and gazing afar.
The clouds unintentionally drift from the mountain peaks,
and the birds, tired of flying, know to return.
The light grows dim as the sun is about to set,
and I stroke a solitary pine tree and linger.
Return, oh, return!
Let me cease social interactions and cut off associations.
The world and I are at odds,
so whom shall I seek by setting out again?
I delight in the heartfelt talks with my relatives,
and find joy in the zither and books to dispel my worries.
The farmers tell me that spring has arrived,
and soon there will be work to do in the western fields.
Some order a covered carriage,
while others row a solitary boat.
We search for valleys in winding paths,
and travel the hills with rugged steps.
The trees flourish and grow,
and the springs trickle and begin to flow.
I rejoice that all things have found their season,
and feel that my life is nearing its end.
Enough!
How much longer shall I dwell within this universe?
Why not entrust my heart and let things take their course?
Why rush around, wanting to go somewhere?
Wealth and high position are not my desire,
and the capital of the Emperor cannot be hoped for.
I cherish the fine days and go out alone,
sometimes planting my staff and weeding the fields.
I climb the eastern hill and whistle freely,
standing by the clear stream and composing poetry.
I will simply follow the process of change and return to the end,
delighting in the mandate of Heaven; what more should I doubt?

Skillful action invites disaster,
and spiteful arguments invite trouble.
Alas, Hán Shēng,
died in the end because of the difficulty of persuasion.
Two Confucian Scholars of Lǔ
*Two Confucian Scholars of Lǔ*
Changing dynasties and following the times,
to be lost in change is foolish.
Upright like those men,
especially true gentlemen.
Virtue cannot last a hundred years,
and will stain our poetry and books.
They left without looking back,
wearing coarse clothes and living in seclusion.
Zhāng Chánggōng
*Zhāng Chánggōng*
Far away is Chánggōng,
serene and without affairs.
The paths of the world are many and complex,
but all are different for me.
I gathered the reins and came here,
cultivating my ambition alone.
Hiding my tracks and living out my years,
who knows this intention?
*Rhapsody on Feeling Unappreciated, with Preface*
Formerly, Dǒng Zhòngshū composed the *Rhapsody on Feeling Unappreciated*,
and Sīmǎ Zǐcháng also wrote one.
I once, during my spare time,
while not lecturing and studying,
read their works,
and felt deeply melancholy and despondent.
To act with trustworthiness and think in accordance with the Way,
is the good conduct of a living person;
to embrace simplicity and preserve stillness,
is the sincere character of a gentleman.
Since the departure of true virtue,
great falsehoods have arisen,
the common people neglect the principles of integrity and humility,
and the marketplace and court drive forward the desire for advancement.
Scholars who cherish righteousness and aspire to the Way,
may hide their jade in their youth;
those who purify themselves and maintain their integrity,
may toil in vain until the end of their lives.
Therefore, Yí and Hào had sighs of where to return,
and Sānlǘ uttered cries of "it is finished!"
Alas!
To reside in form for a hundred years,
and to exhaust it in the blink of an eye;
the difficulty of establishing conduct,
and not a single city appreciates it.
This is why the ancients took up their brushes with emotion,
expressing themselves repeatedly and unable to stop.
To guide and convey one's feelings,
what else but writing?
Stroking the scroll and hesitating,
I thus felt moved and composed this rhapsody.
I inquire of the Great Clod receiving Qi,
why is this person uniquely intelligent!
Endowed with divine wisdom to conceal and illuminate,
possessing outstanding qualities to pass down a name.
Some strike the earth with clods to amuse themselves,
others greatly aid the common people;
nothing that is neither hidden nor leaping goes beyond their allotted share,
they are always proudly contented.
The world flows turbulently and then vanishes,
things are divided into groups and compared in appearance.
When the fine net is cast, the fish are frightened,
when the large net is laid, the birds are alarmed.
Those enlightened ones who are good at perceiving,
then flee from emolument and return to farming.
The mountains stand tall and embrace shadows,
the rivers stretch boundlessly and conceal sounds.
Gazing at Xuāntáng, one sighs eternally,
embracing poverty and lowliness to reject honor.
The pure source gurgles, branching out far,
good and evil arise, diverging into different paths.
Considering what is most valued among all virtues,
nothing is more delightful than doing good.
Accepting the accomplished mandate of Upper Heaven,
learning from the bequeathed writings of sages.
Expressing loyalty and filial piety to ruler and parents,
fostering trustworthiness and righteousness in the neighborhood.
Proffering sincerity and gaining renown,
not acting pretentiously to seek praise.
Alas!
People echo each other, destroying what is different,
things dislike their superiors,
those skilled in calculation are called deluded,
those who follow the straight path are called foolish.
Displaying utter impartiality without suspicion,
in the end one suffers shame and receives slander.
Though holding jade and grasping orchids,
purely fragrant and pure, who will appreciate them.
Alas!
That a scholar does not meet with fortune,
is no longer the age of Yándì Dì Kuí.
Diligently cultivating oneself in solitude,
how can one fail to examine oneself three times a day;
hoping to advance in virtue in a timely manner,
when the time comes, there is no kindness.
Without the discerning words of Yuán Shēng,
I think of Zhāng Jì's ultimate obscurity;
pitying the old man Féng at the Láng office,
relying on Prefect Wèi to accept his plan.
Though barely arriving at what one must know,
it also entails painstaking effort and many years.
Understanding that there are no tigers in the market,
bewilderingly presenting the sayings of three men.
Lamenting the talent and brilliance of Master Jiǎ,
yielding the distant reins in a narrow domain.
Grieving for the deep understanding of Chancellor Dǒng,
repeatedly facing danger but fortunately surviving.
Moved by the unmatched wisdom of the wise,
tears flow copiously and wet my sleeves.
Receiving the clear teachings of former kings,
which say that the Way of Heaven is impartial;
clarifying and obtaining unity to serve as a mirror,
constantly assisting goodness and blessing benevolence.
Yí starved until old age,
Huí died young and was also poor;
saddened by requesting a cart to prepare a coffin,
grieving over eating ferns and dying;
though loving learning and practicing righteousness,
why is death and life so bitter!
Suspecting that repaying virtue is like this,
fearing that these words are empty and exaggerated.
Why is there a lack of talent across the ages,
rarely is there a road that is not difficult.
Oh, the magnanimity of the ancients,
lamenting the failure to establish an extraordinary reputation.
Having bound his hair to participate in politics,
he was not ashamed of being rewarded in myriad cities;
suppressing his heroic ambitions to petty servants,
ultimately not even a foot of land was attainable.
Leaving sincerity and trustworthiness behind,
lamenting the mourning and weeping of the multitude.
Shāng exhausted his plans to rectify abuses,
his words initially went smoothly, but then disaster entered.
Why is a good time so easily overturned,
how can harm win so quickly.
The blue sky is distant and vast,
human affairs never cease.
There is feeling and there is ignorance,
who can fathom its reason.
I would rather solidify my poverty to realize my intentions,
than compromise myself and burden myself.
Since official hats and carriages are not truly glorious,
how could wearing hemp robes be shameful.
Truly, I mistakenly gathered together to appear clumsy,
and now I happily return and stop.
Embracing my solitary feelings to finish my days,
I bid farewell to good prices in the court and market.
"Fu on Leisurely Feelings"
Initially, Zhāng Héng composed the "Fu on Settling Affections",
Cài Yōng composed the "Fu on Tranquil Feelings",
examining unrestrained words and following tranquility,
beginning with wandering thoughts and considerations,
and ultimately returning to leisure and correctness.
Intended to suppress the licentious heart of drifting,
it can truly assist in admonition.
Scholars who string together words,
succeeding each other through generations,
all through touching on similar things,
expand its words and meaning.
I have much leisure in my village neighborhood,
and again take up the brush to write it.
Though the writing is not brilliant enough,
perhaps it does not misunderstand the intention of the authors?
Oh, what a beautiful figure Huái Yì possessed!
Unique in her generation, surpassing all others in elegance.
Displaying beauty that could topple cities,
hoped to be known for her virtue.
Her jade ornaments echoed her purity,
competing in fragrance with the secluded orchids;
holding gentle emotions within,
bearing noble aspirations in the high clouds.
Grieving that the morning sun easily turns to evening,
feeling that life is long and toilsome.
We all meet our end within a hundred years,
so why is joy so scarce and sorrow so abundant?
She lifted the red curtain and sat upright,
playing the clear zither to please herself;
sending forth the beauty of her slender fingers,
and the fluttering of her white sleeves.
Her beautiful eyes flashed as she glanced around,
holding back laughter and words.
As the melody was about to reach its midpoint,
the sunlight fell on the western veranda.
The sorrowful Shāng tone struck the forest,
white clouds clung to the mountains.
Looking up, I gazed at the heavenly path,
looking down, I urged on the sounding strings.
Her divine appearance was charming and graceful,
her manner refined and beautiful.
The clear sound stirred my heart,
I wished to draw near and speak with her.
I wanted to go and pledge my love,
but feared it would be impolite and improper.
I waited for a phoenix to convey my message,
but feared someone else would get to her first.
My heart was anxious and restless,
my soul wandered restlessly.
I wished to be the collar of her dress,
to receive the remaining fragrance of her beautiful head;
sad that the silk collar would be taken off at night,
resenting the endless autumn night.
I wished to be the sash of her skirt,
to bind her slender and graceful waist;
lamenting the change in temperature,
sometimes cast aside for something new.
I wished to be the oil for her hair,
to smooth her dark tresses over her drooping shoulders;
sad that the beauty would bathe so often,
subjecting herself to boiling water.
I wished to be the dark eyebrow pigment,
following her gaze as it leisurely rises and falls;
sad that the rouge and powder would still be fresh,
yet might be ruined by elaborate makeup.
I wished to be the rush mat,
to comfort her delicate body in the autumn season;
sad that the embroidered cushion would replace me,
only to be sought after once a year.
I wished to be the silk of her slippers,
to follow her bare feet as she moved about;
sad that her movements were restrained,
left abandoned before the bed.
I wished to be her shadow in the daytime,
always following her form, east and west;
sad that the tall trees would cast many shadows,
regretting that we could not always be together.
I wished to be the candle at night,
illuminating her jade-like face between the two pillars;
sad that when the Fúsāng tree spreads its light,
it would quickly extinguish my glow and hide my brightness.
I wished to be the bamboo of her fan,
containing the chilling breeze in her gentle grasp;
sad that the white dew would fall in the morning,
causing her to look at her sleeves with longing.
I wished to be the wood of her qín,
becoming the instrument played on her lap;
sad that joy would turn to sorrow,
eventually pushing me away and stopping the music.
My wishes always turned out contrary,
leaving me with a burdened and bitter heart.
Holding onto my weary feelings without complaint,
I strolled leisurely through the southern grove.
Resting among the remaining dew on the magnolias,
shaded by the lingering shadows of the green pines.
Hoping that by walking, I might encounter her,
feeling both joy and fear in my heart.
But in the end, there was only silence,
leaving me alone with my longing and empty searching.
I gathered my light skirt and returned,
gazing at the setting sun with a sigh.
Wandering aimlessly, I forgot my joy,
my face pale and sorrowful.
Leaves fell from the branches,
the air grew cold and bleak.
The sun carried its shadow and disappeared,
the moon displayed its beauty on the clouds.
Birds cried mournfully as they returned home alone,
beasts sought their mates but could not find them.
I grieved for the lateness of the year,
regretting that this time was coming to an end.
I thought of following her in my dreams at night,
but my spirit was restless and uneasy.
Like a boat without a rudder,
like climbing a cliff with nothing to hold on to.
At that time, the stars Bì and Mǎo filled the sky,
and the north wind was cold.
Anxious and unable to sleep,
my mind was filled with thoughts.
I got up, straightened my belt, and waited for dawn,
and saw the thick frost shining on the white steps.
The rooster had folded its wings but not yet crowed,
and the flute played a distant, clear, and mournful tune,
beginning gently and harmoniously,
ending with emptiness and sorrow.
I imagined that lady was here,
entrusting her longing to the drifting clouds.
But the drifting clouds departed without a word,
and time passed slowly.
I only burdened myself with sorrowful thoughts,
ultimately separated by mountains and rivers.
I welcomed the clear breeze to dispel my weariness,
and entrusted my weak will to the returning waves.
Especially when the creeping plants flourish,
I recite the remaining songs of Shào Nán.
I opened my heart to all thoughts to preserve sincerity,
and rested my distant feelings in the eight directions.
In Praise of *The Classic of Filial Piety of the Son of Heaven*
Yú Shùn, Xià Yǔ, Yīn Gāo Zōng, Zhōu Wén Wáng.
Yú Shùn had a stubborn father and a nagging mother;
he served them among the fields,
with utmost filial piety;
therefore, Yáo heard of him and entrusted him with power.
Rich in the world,
noble as the Son of Heaven,
he believed that being disobedient to one's parents
was like being poor and without a home.
Only by being obedient to one's parents could one find satisfaction.
If one disobeyed them even for a moment,
it would be like an infant yearning for its mother.
Therefore, it is said that Shùn was still longing for them at fifty.
The *Book of Documents* says:
“Strike the sounding stone,
beat the qín and sè to sing,
that the ancestral spirits may come.”
This means to think of them coming and to instruct them.
Love and respect were fully expressed in serving his parents,
therefore, his virtuous teachings extended to the people,
serving as a model for the world.
Xià Yǔ possessed the world,
in order to serve the ancestral temples,
yet he himself lived frugally,
to enhance his filial piety.
Confucius said:
“Yǔ,
I can find no fault in him.
He reduced his food and drink to show filial piety to the spirits,
and wore simple clothing to enhance the beauty of the ceremonial robes.”
Yǔ's virtue was therefore widely praised.
There is no virtue of a sage
greater than filial piety and respect,
and in the way of filial piety and respect,
there is no greater beauty.
Yīn Gāo Zōng was in mourning,
and for three years he did not speak.
The officials took charge and listened to the chief minister,
and after three years he spoke,
and the world rejoiced.
His virtuous teachings greatly spread,
and the Yīn dynasty prospered.
The *Book of Songs* says:
“When one person is blessed,
the myriad people rely on him.”
This is what it means!
When Zhōu Wén Wáng was still the heir apparent,
he paid his respects to Wáng Jì three times a day.
From the crowing of the rooster until he reached the gate of the bedchamber,
he would ask the inner attendant,
and if the inner attendant said, “He is well,”
Wén Wáng would rejoice;
if he said, “He is not well,”
his face would show worry,
and he would not walk properly.
At midday and evening,
he would do the same.
When food was served,
he would always check the temperature;
when food was removed,
he would always ask what was eaten before having it taken away.
Wén Wáng's filial piety was glorious and great,
his influence spread from near to far,
serving as a model for his wife,
and governing his family and state.
Therefore, he gained the hearts of all the states,
and served his ancestors well.
The eulogy says:
How perfect was the virtue of the queen!
Her sacred reverence came from Heaven.
She employed pottery and fishing to provide sustenance,
and meager offerings to honor her ancestors.
She grieved over the people's thinness and showed concern,
dwelling in a simple hut and carefully choosing her words.
One person's blessing
is relied upon by thousands of years to come.
"Eulogies for the Filial Conduct of the Lords"
Zhōu Gōng Dàn, Lǔ Xiào Gōng, Héjiān Huì Wáng.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was
the younger brother of Wǔ Wáng.
When Chéng Wáng was young,
Zhōu Gōng administered the government,
establishing rites and creating music,
sacrificing to Hòujì in the suburbs to match Heaven,
and venerating Wén Wáng in the Mingtang (Bright Hall)
to match the Supreme Deity.
Therefore, within the four seas,
each came to offer sacrifices according to their duty.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"Oh, the solemn and pure temple,
Respectful and harmonious, the illustrious assistants!"
This speaks of the lords delighting in their positions and revering their duties.
Zhòngní (Confucius) said:
"There is no greater filial piety than honoring one's father,
and no greater way to honor one's father than to match him with Heaven."
This describes Zhōu Gōng,
noble yet not arrogant,
high in position yet even more humble,
inheriting the fine legacy of Wén and Wǔ,
his filial piety reaching the spirits,
and his virtue spreading to the four seas.
Wǔ Wáng enfeoffed him in Lǔ,
providing him with the complete rites and music
to venerate the ancestral temples there.
When Lǔ Xiào Gōng was still a son of the ruler,
Zhōu Xuān Wáng asked who among the sons could guide and instruct the lords to establish them.
Fán Mùzhòng praised his filial piety, saying:
"He reverently honors the spirits
and respectfully serves the elders.
When assigning duties or executing punishments,
he always asks about past instructions
and consults old precedents.
He does not interfere with what he asks
nor violate what he consults."
The king said:
"Then he can certainly govern and manage his people."
So he appointed him in Yí Palace,
and he became Xiào Gōng.
To show respect in the ancestral temple
is to not forget one's parents;
is it not fitting that he should have a state?
The Hàn Héjiān Huì Wáng
was the great-grandson of Xiàn Wáng.
Among the Han court vassals of Xījīng (Western Capital),
many were guilty of arrogance and excess,
but among those of virtuous reputation
was Xiàn Wáng,
and Huì Wáng continued his legacy.
The *Hàn Shū* (Book of Han) praises his ability to cultivate the conduct of Xiàn Wáng.
When his mother passed away,
he observed the mourning rites completely.
Emperor Āi issued an edict praising him,
considering him a model for the imperial clan,
and increased his fief by ten thousand households.
Such rites
were common among the ancients,
but now in these degenerate times,
it is truly virtuous,
and it is especially difficult for the noble to lead with rites.
Is it not fitting that he should be praised and rewarded?
The eulogy says:
Nobility and arrogance take different paths,
but they meet unexpectedly.
Zhōu Gōng's labor and humility
led to great success.
The two lords who succeeded in Lǔ
followed frugality and rejected extravagance.
Héjiān led with rites,
and the Hàn imperial clan relied on him.
"Eulogies for the Filial Conduct of Ministers and Great Officers"
Kǒngzǐ, Mèng Zhuāngzǐ, Yǐng Kǎoshū.
Kǒngzǐ
was a man of Lǔ.
At home, he served his father and elder brothers;
abroad, he served dukes and ministers.
In mourning affairs, he dared not be remiss.
Thus, it was said:
"Filial piety, oh, filial piety!
Friendly to brothers!
This is also acting as government."
When the ruler bestowed raw meat,
he would surely cook it and offer it to his ancestors.
Even with simple vegetarian meals, he would be reverent,
and his sacrifices were as if they were present.
During the village exorcism ceremony,
he would stand in court attire on the eastern steps,
showing the utmost filial piety.
Of the essential principles of virtue and the Way,
none is greater than filial piety.
Therefore, Zēng Shēn received and wrote it down.
The disciples Zǐyóu and Zixià
often sought his guidance.
Xǔ Zhǐ did not taste medicine,
and was recorded as having killed his father.
Zǎi Yǔ briefly suggested reducing the mourning period
and was rebuked for being unbenevolent.
His words were in accordance with instructional texts,
and his actions were in accordance with worldly models.
His virtue and righteousness are worthy of respect,
his actions are worthy of emulation,
his surviving writings are imperishable,
and his name will be known for thousands of years.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ
was a man of Lǔ.
Kǒngzǐ said that he might be good at other things,
but his most remarkable trait was
not changing his father's policies
or his father's ministers,
which was truly difficult to achieve.
The way a filial son serves his parents
is to serve the dead as if they were alive.
Therefore, when something is unrighteous, he will argue against it,
but what he does not argue against while they are alive,
he will not dare to change after their death.
Not changing the way of one's father for three years
is still considered filial piety,
let alone for a lifetime.
Yǐng Kǎoshū
was a man of Zhèng.
Because of Shū Duàn, Duke Zhuāng
made a vow to his mother, saying:
"Unless we reach the Yellow Springs,
we shall never see each other."
Later, he regretted it.
Kǎoshū was a border official
and heard of this.
He had something to offer the duke,
and the duke gave him food,
but he set the meat aside.
The duke asked him why,
and he replied:
"I have a mother
who has never tasted the duke's soup,
so I ask to leave it for her."
The duke said:
"You have a mother to give it to,
but alas, I alone do not!"
Kǎoshū asked:
"What do you mean?"
The duke told him the story
and confessed his regret.
Kǎoshū said:
"If you dig a tunnel to the spring and meet there,
who would say it is not so?"
The duke followed his advice,
and thus mother and son were as they had been before.
A gentleman said:
"Yǐng Kǎoshū
was truly filial,
loving his mother and extending that love to Duke Zhuāng."
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"A filial son is never lacking,
Granting good fortune to you and your descendants."
Is this not what it means?
The eulogy says:
Benevolence takes brotherly love as its root,
and sagehood is also based on filial piety.
The gentle Ní Fù (Confucius)
was indeed created by Heaven.
The two gentlemen served their parents,
following rites and obeying instructions.
Granting lasting purity and excellence,
they did not change the legacy of their fathers.
"Eulogies for the Filial Conduct of Scholars"
Gāo Chái, Yuèzhèng Zichūn, Kǒng Fèn, Huáng Xiāng.
Gāo Chái,
was a person from Wèi.
Upon the death of his parents,
he wept blood for three years,
and never showed his teeth [by smiling],
which is what is meant by "weeping without wailing affectation,
and speaking without elaborate language."
He served as the magistrate of Wǔchéng and transformed its customs,
reforming those people who did not treat their parents well,
and having them observe mourning rites properly.
The virtue of a ruler is like the wind,
leading the way by personal example,
so that the people do not neglect their parents.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn,
was a person from Lǔ.
Once, descending from the hall, he injured his foot.
After he recovered,
he did not go out for several months,
and still looked worried.
He said:
"I heard from Zēngzǐ that,
'to be born with one's body whole from one's parents,
and to return it whole [at death],
may be called filial piety.'
Therefore, a gentleman's every step
and every word
never forgets his parents,
and he dares not cause injury or damage [to his body];
this is the beginning of filial piety."
If one can be so respectful and careful as this,
and yet calamity and misfortune befall him,
that has never happened.
Kǒng Fèn,
was a person from Fúfēng.
From a young age, he was known throughout the region for his filial conduct,
and he provided for his parents with utmost care.
While in office,
only his mother enjoyed the most delicious foods,
while his wife and children ate only vegetables.
He advanced through the ranks because of his incorruptibility.
In human nature, there is no one who does not wish to treat their parents well,
but there are also limitations;
extravagance is difficult to sustain,
and those who can maintain frugality to fully provide for their parents
are few.
Huáng Xiāng,
was a person from Jiāngxià.
He lost his mother at the age of nine,
and his longing for her caused him to become gaunt.
He served his father with all his strength to provide for him,
not wearing padded trousers in winter and exhausting every delicacy for his father,
and fanning his bed and pillow in the summer,
and warming the bed with his body in the winter.
Emperor Hé of the Hàn dynasty praised him,
and bestowed upon him special favors.
Throughout his career, he was respectful and diligent,
bringing honor to his parents with his position and emoluments,
truly embodying the saying "rising early and sleeping late,
not disgracing those who gave you life."
The eulogy says:
"These outstanding gentlemen,
have different deeds but equal reputations.
All are able to be diligent day and night,
to bring honor to their parents through righteousness.
Leading their cities and towns,
they use their example to transform their people.
Their loyalty awakens their lords,
and their filial piety is pure."
*Eulogies for the Filial Conduct of Commoners*
Jiāng Gé, Lián Fàn, Rǔ Yù, Yīn Táo.
Jiāng Gé
was a person from Qí.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of the Hàn dynasty,
he carried his mother on his back to escape from bandits.
The bandits recognized his virtue
and did not harm him, and told him the way to survive.
He worked hard as a laborer,
in order to provide his mother with delicious food and warm clothing,
always maintaining a pleasant and cheerful demeanor
to bring her joy.
Wishing for his mother's comfort,
he pulled the cart himself.
The villagers admired him
and called him "Jiāng the Greatly Filial."
He rose to the position of Commandant of the Five Offices,
and the Emperor commended him,
treating him with great favor.
When he requested to retire,
the imperial edict praised him,
and he was treated with respect in his home for the rest of his life,
to show his extraordinary conduct.
Lián Fàn
was a person from Jīngzhào.
He was orphaned at a young age.
At fifteen, he entered Shǔ
to retrieve his father's coffin.
He encountered a capsized stone boat.
Fàn clung to the coffin and sank with it.
The boatmen rescued him
and he barely escaped death,
and then carried the coffin back home.
When he served as an official, he rescued the Grand Administrator from danger,
offering his services to the deceased with utmost loyalty.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng, he served as Grand Administrator,
and the people sang his praises.
Filial piety
is the root of humanity,
and the origin of all teachings.
Therefore, Fàn was brave in times of danger,
and benevolent in governing the people,
able to distinguish himself through righteousness.
Rǔ Yù
was a person from Chénjùn.
At the age of five,
his mother fell ill and could not eat,
and Yù also refused to eat.
His mother pitied him
and urged him to eat.
Yù could discern her expression
and knew her illness,
and so refused to eat again.
The family called him "the extraordinary child."
At the age of fifteen,
he became known throughout the region.
After his parents passed away,
his longing for them caused him to become emaciated.
He gave his wealth to his brothers
and lived in seclusion in the wilderness,
which gentlemen considered difficult to do.
How much more commendable that a young child should be filial by nature,
which may be called innate.
Yīn Táo
was a person from Rǔnán.
At the age of twelve,
he was known for his filial piety.
When he encountered the death of his father,
he acted in accordance with his feelings and the rites.
A long snake entered his gate,
and the whole family fled in panic.
Táo, because the coffin was there,
remained alone in the hut and did not move.
His relatives supported and explained to him,
but none could move him,
and his cries grew even louder.
Because of this, he became famous
and repeatedly declined appointments.
The wise are not perplexed,
and the brave are not afraid.
Táo was filial to his parents,
and his wisdom and courage were evident at a young age,
which is even more difficult.
The eulogy says:
"To serve one's parents with complete joy,
the difficulty lies in one's countenance.
Others provide with emoluments,
we provide with our strength.
Righteousness lies in love and respect,
honor needs no embellishment.
Alas, all of you,
take heed of these former examples."

*Eulogy for Younger Sister Chéng 程*
In the third year of Yìxī of the Jìn dynasty,
on the day jiǎchén in the fifth month,
the mourning period for the younger sister of the Chéng family had passed its second cycle.
Yuānmíng, with a small offering,
bowed and poured a libation.
Alas, woe is me!
The cold departs and the heat arrives,
the days and months gradually become distant.
Dust accumulates on the rafters,
weeds grow wild in the courtyard.
The empty room is desolate,
the orphaned children are mournful.
Food and wine are placed as offerings,
but the person has departed, never to return!
Who is without brothers and sisters?
People are born alike,
but alas, the situation between you and me
is particularly beyond ordinary feelings.
Our kind mother passed away early,
when we were still young children.
I was twenty-six years old,
and you were only nine.
We have been together since we were unable to discern,
growing up together from our childhood.
Alas, your excellent younger sister,
possessed virtue and integrity.
She was respectful, reserved in speech,
and delighted in hearing of good deeds.
Capable of being righteous and harmonious,
she was both friendly and filial.
Her conduct was confined to the inner chambers,
a model to be emulated.
I heard that doing good
brings joy to oneself.
Why is Heaven so biased,
as not to reward her?
Once in Jiānglíng,
we suffered another calamity.
Brothers and sisters lived separately,
divided like the lands of Chǔ and Yuè.
You and I,
a hundred sorrows cut deep.
Dark and gloomy were the high clouds,
desolate was the winter month.
White snow covered the morning,
a long wind lamented the season.
I felt like collapsing and wailing,
speaking out and weeping blood.
Thinking back to the past,
everything still feels so recent.
Letters and documents still remain,
orphaned children fill my eyes.
How can one departure
mean never returning for eternity!
The silent and empty hall,
when will I ever tread upon it again?
The insignificant orphaned girl,
on whom shall she rely?
The lonely wandering soul,
who will preside over and perform sacrifices?
Alas, sister Chéng,
she has ended here forever!
If the dead have knowledge,
we shall meet in Hāolǐ.
Alas, woe is me!
"Eulogy for My Cousin Jìngyuǎn"
In the year xīnhài,
in the mid-autumn month,
on the nineteenth day of the month,
my cousin Jìngyuǎn,
having chosen a propitious day for burial,
rests eternally in the soil.
I am saddened by our shared past,
and grieved by the departure from which there is no return.
My heart is torn with sorrow,
and tears fill my eyes with grief.
Therefore, with garden fruits and seasonal wine,
I bid farewell to his departure.
Alas, woe is me!
Oh, my excellent cousin,
you possessed integrity and principles.
Filial piety arose in your early years,
friendship came naturally through divine favor.
You had few desires and little ambition,
without clinging or prejudice.
Putting others before yourself,
you considered giving when facing wealth.
Your heart disregarded personal gain or loss,
your emotions were not bound by the world.
Your demeanor was warm,
your words were stern.
You delighted in surpassing your esteemed friends,
and cherished literary pursuits.
Far away was the celestial realm,
inspiring a unique longing in your heart.
You abstained from grains and relinquished worldly affairs,
retiring to the mountains of Shānyīn.
Rushing was the flowing spring,
dim and hazy was the desolate forest.
In the morning you gathered medicinal herbs,
in the evening you idled with your simple zither.
It is said that the benevolent live long,
and I secretly believed this.
How could these words
simply deceive us!
Barely past thirty,
you suddenly departed from the world.
You returned forever to Hāolǐ,
never to return.
You and I,
were not only relatives and friends.
Our fathers were born of the same father,
our mothers were cousins.
We reached our childhood together,
both afflicted by misfortune.
Our affection was truly deep,
our love was truly profound.
Thinking of days of old,
the joy of sharing a room.
In winter, we lacked lined clothes,
in summer, we thirsted for a gourd of water.
We guided each other with principles,
we cheered each other with smiles.
Though we often lacked much,
we would forget hunger and cold.
I once studied for officialdom,
entangled in worldly affairs.
Wandering without success,
I feared betraying my original ambition.
Ceasing my efforts and returning home,
you knew my intentions.
I always wished to hold hands with you,
and set aside worldly desires.
I often recall the autumn,
when I would harvest the crops.
Walking together with you,
we crossed the river in the same boat.
Staying three nights by the water,
we joyfully drank by the riverbank.
The silent moon shone high,
the gentle breeze began to cease.
Holding our cups, we spoke of how
things are fragile and people are fleeting.
Alas, my cousin,
you departed from the world before me!
The past cannot be found,
thoughts are boundless.
Days pass and months flow,
cold and heat alternate.
Life and death are in different realms,
existence and demise have boundaries.
Awaiting the dawn, you return forever,
pointing the way, we ascend the path.
The crying orphaned child,
cannot yet speak properly.
The grieving widow,
is well-versed in ritual and propriety.
The trees in the courtyard remain as before,
the study is quiet and empty.
Who says Jìngyuǎn
will ever return?
I, though a person,
am ignorant of these intimate feelings.
The divination with milfoil stalks and tortoise shell yielded auspicious results,
ordaining my journey to bid farewell.
Gazing at the fluttering banners,
I hold the brush, tears filling my eyes.
May your spirit be aware,
and understand my inner sincerity.
Alas, woe is me!
"Self-Eulogy"
The year was Dīngmǎo,
the month corresponded to Wúshè.
The sky was cold, and the night was long;
the wind and air were bleak.
The wild geese were on their journey,
and the grasses and trees turned yellow and fell.
Táo Zǐ was about to leave the transient inn
and return forever to his original home.
His old friends were sorrowful and grieved,
accompanying his funeral procession this evening.
We offer fine vegetables
and present clear wine.
His appearance is already darkened,
and his voice grows ever more distant.
Alas!
Vast and boundless is the great earth,
distant and endless is the high sky.
It produces all things;
I was fortunate to become a man.
Since I became a man,
I have encountered misfortune.
My bamboo basket and gourd are often empty,
and hemp clothes are laid out in winter.
I gladly draw water from the valley,
and sing as I carry firewood on my back.
My humble thatched door
serves me from night until morning.
Spring and autumn alternate,
and I am busy in my garden.
I plow and plant,
then nurture and propagate.
I happily play with plain books,
and harmonize with the seven-stringed zither.
In winter, I bask in the sun;
in summer, I wash in the spring.
My toil is without excessive labor,
and my heart has constant leisure.
I happily entrust myself to fate,
to live to be a hundred years old.
These hundred years,
people cherish them.
Fearing they will achieve nothing,
they begrudge the days and cherish the time.
Alive, they are treasures of the world;
dead, they are remembered with longing.
Alas, I alone go my own way,
have I ever been different from this?
Favor is not my glory,
and can mud stain my black silk?
I stumble about in my poor hut,
drink heartily and compose poems.
Knowing fate and understanding destiny,
who can fail to care?
Now that I am transformed,
I can be without regrets.
My life has reached a hundred years;
my body has longed for a reclusive retreat.
Having lived to old age and reached my end,
what else should I yearn for?
The cold and heat pass by;
death is different from life.
Distant relatives come in the morning,
and good friends rush here at night.
Bury him in the wilderness
to give peace to his soul.
Dimly I walk,
bleak is the tomb gate.
The extravagance of the Sòng臣,
and the frugality mocked by the Wángsūn.
Vastly he is gone,
deeply he is far away.
Neither mound nor tree,
the days and months pass.
Not valuing former praise,
who cares about later songs?
Life is truly difficult;
how is death?
Alas!

King Wēi of Qí and King Huì of Wèi met
and hunted in the suburbs.
The King of Wèi asked King Wēi, saying:
"Does Your Majesty have treasures?"
King Wēi said:
"I have none."
The King of Wèi said:
"As for me,
though my state is small,
I still have ten pearls of one inch in diameter,
each of which can illuminate twelve carriages in front and behind.
How can a state of ten thousand chariots have no treasures?"
King Wēi said:
"The reason I regard something as treasure
is different from Your Majesty.
I have a minister named Tán Zǐ,
whom I sent to guard the southern city,
and the people of Chǔ dare not invade.
He seized the territory above the Sì River to the east,
and twelve lords all came to court.
I have a minister named Pàn Zǐ,
whom I sent to guard Gāo Táng,
and the people of Wèi dare not fish east of the river.
I have a minister named Qián Fū,
whom I sent to guard Xú,
and the people of Yàn sacrifice at the north gate,
and the people of Zhào sacrifice at the west gate,
and more than seventy families move to follow them.
I have a minister named Zhǒng Shǒu,
whom I sent to guard against thieves and bandits,
and things dropped on the road are not picked up.
Regarding these as treasures,
they will illuminate a thousand chariots;
how can they merely illuminate twelve chariots?"
King Huì of Wèi was ashamed
and left displeased.

"The Eight *Rú*"
After Master Kǒng passed away,
they dispersed throughout the world,
were established in the central states,
became the source of the hundred schools,
and were *rú* of cardinal principles.
Dwelling in a room of only a few square feet,
with a thatched door and a small window like a hole,
a broken jar as a window and a rope as a hinge,
eating only once every two days,
and taking the Dao as their dwelling,
these are the *rú* of the Dao,
the practice of Zisi.
Wearing the proper attire,
acting respectfully,
giving way greatly as if reluctant,
and yielding slightly as if falsely,
this is the practice of Zizhang.
The Yán school transmitted the *Shī* as the Dao,
being *rú* of satire and remonstrance.
The Mèng school transmitted the *Shū* as the Dao,
being *rú* who explore widely and achieve distant goals.
The Qīdiao school transmitted the *Lǐ* as the Dao,
being *rú* of reverence, frugality, solemnity, and respect.
The Zhòngliáng school transmitted the *Yuè* as the Dao,
harmonizing yin and yang,
being *rú* who change customs and transform habits.
The Yuèzhèng school transmitted the *Chūnqiū* as the Dao,
being *rú* who construct phrases and compare events.
The Gōngsūn school transmitted the *Yì* as the Dao,
being *rú* of purity, cleanliness, refinement, and subtlety.
"The Three Mò"
Not burdened by customs,
not adorned by things,
not honoring fame,
not envying the masses:
this is the Mò of Sòng Xíng and Yǐn Wén.
Wearing sheepskin and coarse cloth as clothing,
and straw sandals as attire,
not resting day or night,
and taking self-affliction as the ultimate:
this is the Mò of Xiànglǐ Qín and Wǔ Hóuzi.
All claiming the *Jīng*, but with divergent doctrines,
they call each other "Separate Mò" based on solidity and whiteness:
this is the Mò of Kǔ Huò, Sì Chǐ, and Dènglíngzi.

"Shàng Chángqín Qìng Zàn"
Master Shàng once had a humble position,
with his wife and children together morning and night.
In poverty and lowliness as in wealth and eminence,
reading the *Yì* he understood increase and decrease.
Qín was born fond of traveling widely,
traveling widely further and further each day.
He left to seek famous mountains,
ascending the mountains, never to return.
